Stiff-person syndrome associated with invasive thymoma: a case report
Hiroki Hagiwara 1, Setsu Enomoto-Nakatani, Katsuyuki Sakai, Yoshikazu Ugawa,
Susumu Kusunoki), Ichiro Kanazawa
Department of Neurology, DiÕision of Neuroscience, Graduate School of Medicine, Uni Õersity of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo, Tokyo, 113-8655, Japan
Received 20 March 2001; received in revised form 6 August 2001; accepted 6 August 2001
Abstract
We report a case of a 40-year-old female with continuous muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms. The symptoms worsened over a
two-week period after onset. Electrophysiological examinations revealed continuous muscle discharge, which was markedly reduced by
Ž.intravenous administration of diazepam. High levels of anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase GAD antibodies were detected in both serum
and cerebrospinal fluid, suggesting that the patient suffered from stiff-person syndrome. Steroid pulse therapy and immunoadsorption
therapy alleviated the clinical symptoms and decreased the anti-GAD antibody titer. A chest CT revealed the presence of an invasive
Ž. Ž .thymoma. Neither anti-acetylcholine receptor AChR antibodies nor symptoms of myasthenia gravis MG were observed. The patient
underwent a thymectomy and postoperative radiotherapy. These treatments further alleviated the clinical symptoms. The present case is
the first that associates stiff-person syndrome with invasive thymoma, and not accompanied by MG. The autoimmune mechanism, in this
case, may be triggered by the invasive thymoma. q 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome is a rare, distressing neurological
disorder that is characterized by continuous systemic mus-
wxcle stiffness and painful paroxysmal muscle spasms 1–3 .
The symptoms usually begin with tightness or stiffness of
the trunk muscles, which may slowly spread to the proxi-
mal muscles of the extremities. In addition to muscle
stiffness, painful paroxysmal muscle spasms are precipi-
tated by sudden movement, sound, tactile stimulation, or
emotional upset. The pathogenesis of the stiff-person syn-
drome is not fully understood. Neuropharmacological stud-
ies have shown evidence of an imbalance between cate-
Ž.cholamine excitatory and g-aminobutyric acid GABA
inhibitory neurotransmitter systems in the brainstem and
spinal cord. In support of this hypothesis, 50–60% of
patients with stiff-person syndrome were reported to have
Ž.autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase GAD ,
which catalyses the conversion of glutamate to GABA,
wxpresent in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid 4,5 . Stiff-

diseases such as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus
Ž.IDDM , Graves’ disease, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, perni-
wxcious anemia 5–7 . In addition, stiff-person syndrome is
reported to be associated with adenocarcinoma of the
breast, adenocarcinoma of the colon, Hodgkin’s lym-
phoma, small-cell carcinoma of the lung, pharyngeal carci-

wxnoma, mediastinal tumor and thymoma 8–14 . Here, we
describe a case of stiff-person syndrome associated with
invasive thymoma that is not accompanied by myasthenia
Ž.gravis MG .
2. Case report
A 40-year-old female clerical worker was admitted to
our hospital complaining of stiffness in the bilateral lower
extremities and a gait disturbance. She has no history of
diabetes, injuries or epilepsy. In addition, there is no
history of intermarriage in her family. Her mother has a
history of dialysis, but details are unknown. The patient’s
life history is unremarkable. On May 22, 1999, the patient
experienced vertigo, pharyngeal pain, dysphagia, and
dysarthria. On May 30, she began to fall backward or
forward repeatedly due to a sudden stiffness of the lower
extremities. On June 2, the patient began to fall forward
due to a sudden stiffness of the abdomen. Around June 4,

maintain a standing or sitting position. Stiffness of the
lower extremities was observed even in a decubitus posi-
tion, and was accompanied by pain. On June 5, the patient
was admitted to our hospital. A general physical examina-
tion on admission revealed no abnormality. A neurological
examination showed that the patient possessed a clear
consciousness. However, her facial expression appeared
agonized, and dysphagia and glossal motor deficits were
observed. During motor nerve examination, the bilateral
lower extremities were observed to be rigid and extended
in an equinovarus position. Painful tonic spasms, dominant
on the right, and myoclonus of the bilateral lower extremi-
ties were observed. These events occurred spontaneously,
or were induced by sensory or acoustic stimuli. Deep
tendon reflexes were increased in the bilateral lower ex-
tremities. Babinski sign was present bilaterally and urinary
urgency was observed.
A laboratory examination on admission showed that the
WBC count was elevated to 10.8 =10

blood cell counts were found to be normal. Serum bio-
chemistry revealed no abnormalities, except that the CK

Ž.was normal in OGTT 75 g . No abnormalities were found
in endocrine functions of ACTH, cortisol and thyroid
hormone. A serological examination revealed that the IgG,
IgM and IgA levels were 1527, 177 and 227 mg rdl,
respectively. Anti-tetanic antibodies were negative. No
Ž.binding or blocking anti-acetylcholine receptor AChR
antibodies were present. Anti-GAD antibodies, anti-gastric
parietal cell antibodies, anti-ssDNA antibody and anti-
Ž.dsDNA antibody were 190,000 U rml normal -0.5 , 20
Ž. Ž. Žnormal -10 , 23.8 normal -20 and 15.7 normal
.-10 , respectively. Anti-pancreatic islet cell antibodies,
anti-thyroid microsomal antibody, anti-thyroglobuline anti-
bodies, anti-mitochondrial antibodies were negative. West-
ern blot analysis, using a serum sample from the patient
and a human brain homogenate revealed no bands near
128 kDa, which is considered to represent amphiphysin
wx8,9 . Tumor markers were negative. In the cerebrospinal
fluid samples, the cell count, the levels of protein and
sugar and the IgG index were 0.3 rml, 19 mg rdl, 72
mgrdl and 0.63, respectively. No oligoclonal band or
myelin basic protein was detected. The anti-GAD antibody
Ž.level was 239 U rml normal -0.5 .
MRI of the head, thoracic and cervical levels of the
spinal cord revealed no abnormality. The electroen-
cephalography was normal. The motor and sensory nerve
conductions were normal. The surface electromyography
detected a continuous muscle discharge in the bilateral
lower extremities, which was markedly reduced during
sleep or with the administration of 10-mg intravenous
diazepam. The clinical course of urinary urgency, dyspha-
gia and glossal motor deficit were alleviated immediately
after hospitalization, on June 5. Stiff-person syndrome was
diagnosed from the clinical course, neurological findings
and other examination results. The patient was treated with
two courses of a three-day pulse therapy, using 1000 mg
methylprednisolone per day, and three courses of im-
munoadsorption therapy. These treatments relieved the

clinical symptoms of muscle stiffness and myoclonus, and
Ždecreased the anti-GAD antibody level 26,900 U rml in
the serum, 91.1 U rml in the cerebrospinal fluid, respec-
.tively . The chest CT, taken to search for malignant tu-
mors, is shown in Fig. 1. The CT revealed the presence of
a3 =2 cm mass with a muscle-like density in the anterior
mediastinum, slightly to the right. The border of the mass
with the aorta was partly unclear. Thus, we concluded that
an invasive thymoma was present. An extended thymec-
tomy was performed on July 26. The pathological findings
of thymectomy are shown in Fig. 2. Lymphocytes were
predominant, and the follicular structure had disappeared.
No heteromorphous nuclei were observed in the thymic
epithelial cells. The segmented tumor had no capsule and
had infiltrated into the fatty tissue, pleura and lung
parenchyma. The tumor was in stage III according to the
wxTNM staging 17 . The thymectomy and postoperative
radiotherapy further alleviated the clinical symptoms of
muscle stiffness and myoclonus. The patient was able to

3. Discussion
In this case, the patient was presented with continuous
muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms that either
occurred spontaneously or were precipitated by sensory
stimuli. Continuous muscle discharge was detected in the
electrophysiological examinations, but these discharges
were markedly decreased by the administration of intra-
venous diazepam. The anti-GAD antibody level was high
in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. The anti-pancreatic
islet cell antibodies were negative. Since islet cells contain
isoforms of GAD, these data seemed to be inconsistent.
We carried out Western blot and found that the antibodies
Ž.reacted with 65-kDa isoform of GAD data not shown .
The discrepancy may be due to differences in sensitivity of
respective analysis. On the basis of the above clinical,
electrophysiological and laboratory findings, stiff-person
syndrome was diagnosed according to the criteria estab-
wx wxlished by Gordon et al. 2 and Lorish et al. 3 . The
bilateral pyramidal sign was present at the time of hospital-
ization, but the deep tendon reflexes became normal and
the Babinski sign became indifferent after intravenous
diazepam treatment. These findings suggest that the spasm
reaction occurs in response to stimuli.
As a differential diagnosis, progressive encephalomyeli-
Ž.tis with rigidity PER may be considered. However, in
this case, higher-cortical functions were maintained, the
cerebrospinal fluid was normal, and the brainstem symp-
toms were temporary while typical PER is progressive.
Neuromyotonia was also ruled out because the symptoms
were not localized in more distal areas and diazepam
should not be as effective as in this case.
Stiff-person syndrome is known to be associated with
autoimmune diseases such as insulin-dependent diabetes
Ž.mellitus IDDM , Graves’ disease, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis,
wxand pernicious anemia 5–7 . In addition, stiff-person syn-
drome is known to be associated with tumors such as
adenocarcinoma of the breast, adenocarcinoma of the colon,
Hodgkin’s lymphoma, small-cell carcinoma of the lung,
pharyngeal carcinoma, mediastinal tumor and thymoma
wx8–14 . However, no large-scale investigation on these
complications has been reported. Grimaldi et al. reported
Žthree cases of autoimmune diseases two cases of IDDM
.and one case of Graves’ disease , four cases of solid tumor
Žone case of colon carcinoma, one case of breast carci-
noma, one case of Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and one case of
. wxthymoma out of 13 cases of stiff-person syndrome 10 .
Only a few reports have associated cases of stiff-person
wxsyndrome with thymoma 12–14 . These cases are summa-
rized in the Table 1. The case reported by Piccolo and Cosi
wx wx12 are identical to those reported by Grimaldi et al. 10 ,
as mentioned above. These cases were accompanied by
Ž. wxmyasthenia gravis MG . Aso et al. 14 reported stiff-per-
son syndrome that was preceded by MG. In the remaining
two cases, MG was reported after the occurrence of stiff-
person syndrome. A pathological examination after thy-
mectomy was conducted only in the case reported by
wxNicholas et al. 13 . In that case, anti-AChR antibodies and
anti-GAD antibodies were not found. The thymoma was
non-invasive and was classified as a cortical type. The

patient developed MG two months after the thymectomy.
Although the thymectomy immediately relieved the symp-
toms of stiff-person syndrome, the symptoms worsened at
the 14th month after surgery. In response to the return of
the symptoms, baclofen and diazepam were administered,
Ž.and intravenous immunoglobulin IVIG treatment was
repeated.
The present case of stiff-person syndrome was found to
be negative for anti-AChR antibodies, but positive for
anti-GAD antibodies. Treatment consisted of steroid pulse
therapy, immunoadsorption therapy, thymectomy and post-
operative radiotherapy. Pathological examinations revealed

that the thymoma was invasive and classified as a pre-
dominantly lymphocytic type. Associated MG has not been
observed. Since the symptoms were further alleviated after
thymectomy, the thymectomy was considered to be effec-
tive for stiff-person syndrome.
Histologically, no heteromorphous nuclei are observed
in the thymic epithelial cells. Therefore, the patient did not
have thymic cancer. Lymphocyte predominancy is the
distinctive pathological feature in this case. The Mayo
Ž.clinic group Lewis et al. has classified thymoma into
subtypes based on cell type. These subtypes include pre-
dominantly lymphocytic, mixed lymphoepithelial, pre-
wxdominantly epithelial, and spindle cell 15 . In contrast,
since normal thymic epithelial cells consist of cortical cells
and medullary cells, Marino and Muller-Hermelink classi-
fied thymoma into the following subtypes based on histo-
genesis: medullary, mixed, predominantly cortical, and
wxcortical 16 . Several reports have demonstrated that corti-
cal thymoma were associated with MG more frequently
wxthan medullary thymoma 18–20 , suggesting that whether
the thymoma is accompanied by MG depend on histologic
features. In thymoma with an MG complication, thymic
epithelial cells are large, clear and polygonal, and lympho-
cytes are present between the cells. These characteristics
are consistent with the cortical type in the Marino and
Muller-Hermelink classification, which includes mixed
lymphoepithelial and predominantly epithelial in Mayo’s
classification. In contrast, thymoma without an MG com-
plication, consists primarily of lymphoid series cells, and
the epithelial cells are spindle-shaped. This is consistent
with the medullary type in the Marino and Muller-Herme-
link classification, which includes predominantly lympho-
cytic and spindle cell types in Mayo’s classification. In
comparing the Nicholas’ case with the present case, the
former corresponds to the cortical type in pathological
findings and is accompanied by MG. In our case, the
pathological findings are predominantly lymphocytic type
and are not accompanied by MG. These findings are
consistent with the above hypothesis. Therefore, the differ-
ent histologic features of thymoma may be predictive of
the onset of MG, and may become a useful indicator to
predict the prognosis of stiff-person syndrome that is
associated with thymoma.
The present case is the first that associates stiff-person
syndrome with invasive thymoma without associated MG.
Stiff-person syndrome, in this case, may be due to the
autoimmune mechanism that is associated with invasive
thymoma.

In our case, the
pathological findings are predominantly lymphocytic type
and are not accompanied by MG. These findings are
consistent with the above hypothesis. Therefore, the differ-
ent histologic features of thymoma may be predictive of
the onset of MG, and may become a useful indicator to
predict the prognosis of stiff-person syndrome that is
associated with thymoma.
The present case is the first that associates stiff-person
syndrome with invasive thymoma without associated MG.
Stiff-person syndrome, in this case, may be due to the
autoimmune mechanism that is associated with invasive
thymoma.
